headline: New law permanently lists fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I drugs and eases some rules for researchers who study these drugs.
what_it_does: The law permanently puts fentanyl-related substances, as a group, in Schedule I, the strictest category of controlled drugs. Crimes involving these substances now carry the same quantity triggers and penalties as crimes involving fentanyl analogues, such as a 10-year mandatory minimum prison sentence for 100 grams or more. It also creates a new, alternative registration process for some Schedule I research and loosens several other registration rules for researchers. It states that Congress agrees with a 2018 court ruling that treated butyryl fentanyl as a fentanyl analogue.

who_it_affects.group: People charged with federal drug crimes involving fentanyl-related substances
who_it_affects.how: They face the same mandatory minimum prison terms and penalties that apply to fentanyl analogue offenses, based on drug quantity.

who_it_affects.group: Scientists and research institutions studying Schedule I drugs
who_it_affects.how: They can use a new alternative registration process, may cover related sites under one registration, may skip a new inspection in some cases, and may do small-scale manufacturing without a separate manufacturing registration.

who_it_affects.group: Federal prosecutors and drug enforcement agencies
who_it_affects.how: They can treat fentanyl-related substances as a permanent Schedule I class rather than relying on temporary scheduling.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted July 16, 2025; the summary does not list a separate start date.
